newsitem.title: BRAZIL: SOCCER-ARGENTINA'S UGLY SIDE BACK ON SHOW.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ARGENTINA'S UGLY SIDE BACK ON SHOW.

text.p: When Argentina walked off with the fair play trophy at last year's Olympic Games it seemed the dark side of their game had finally been consigned to the dustbin of soccer history.
The Argentines had behaved impeccably at the 1994 World Cup -- even in the face of Diego Maradona failing a drugs test -- and better still at the Atlanta Games as they won the silver medal.

But the fighting, play-acting and incessant bickering which has marred Argentine performances at some previous World Cups returned with a vengeance as the two-times world champions lost 2-1 to Bolivia in a World Cup qualifier in La Paz on Wednesday.
Play was held up for more than 10 minutes by a brawl as the Argentines, who earlier had two players sent off, lost their heads.

One player was caught by television cameras spitting in the direction of Bolivian fans while others, visibly wild with rage, tried desperately to get their hands on members of the Bolivian team bench.
And on a day that international soccer's governing body FIFA criticised players who attempted to deceive referees, Argentina showed that play-acting was still part and parcel of their repertoire.
FIFA general secretary Sepp Blatter said earlier: "When a professional star takes a dive, millions of lesser players dive with him." He went on to describe the practice as cheating.
But if Blatter's words reached the Argentine team hotel in the Bolivian capital, they fell on deaf ears.
Throughout the game, Argentina gave the impression that feigning injury is an integral part of their tactics for winning a game.
During the second half, television cameras caught a close up of an argument between Bolivia substitute Demetrio Angola and Argentina's Gustavo Zapata.
Angola's finger made slight contact with Zapata's forehead. The Argentine immediately collapsed and lay on the pitch, clutching his face in apparent agony.

Some of the Argentine tackling was gruesome and despite their complaints over the choice of Brazil's Sidrack Marinho as referee, the only criticism that could be levelled at the official was that he was too lenient.
Argentina were in a negative mood from the moment they arrived in La Paz.

Even though Colombia, Peru, Paraguay and Chile had all obtained draws in previous qualifiers in La Paz, they complained bitterly at having to play in the city which lies at 3,600 metres above sea level.
The day before the game, coach Daniel Passarella had stormed out of a news conference in protest at a question from a local reporter.
It was a return to the dark days of the past which have blighted Argentine soccer.
The country have won the World Cup twice and have graced the game with the skills of players such as Mario Kempes and Maradona.

But fans worldwide remember other images just as vividly: the furious protests at the end of the 1990 World Cup final as two Argentines were sent off; Diego Maradona's notorious "Hand of God" goal in 1986; and the infamous scenes during and after their quarter-final in the 1966 World Cup.
